#### **A double blow**

Easter Monday, March 26, 1951

It must have been 10 o'clock in the morning when Dr Anne Casey, 36, started to worry. Little Laura was bouncing on her big pregnant belly and couldn't be stopped. Normally she'd be in with her daddy in the other room. Anne hauled herself out of bed and waddled over to the mirror-image bedroom occupied by her husband, Dr Michael Augustine Casey, 52.

Austie Casey hadn't been in the best of health for some time and he'd already had two heart attacks. As soon as she opened the door, she let out a yelp, to the horror of the children and anyone else scattered around the house. There he was, dead to the world. He had slipped away in his sleep, painlessly she hoped.

The big house was curiously empty for a festive weekend. By now, Anne had taken to the other room because she was due to have the baby any day. She had her own complications. Oedema, perhaps, or maybe toxemia. But things were not looking good for the baby. Laura Ann had been a miracle and was a ruddy two year old now, the first Rhesus baby in Ireland to survive. She got the all-important blood transfusion, a procedure that had only recently been developed in America. Austie Casey must have had to muscle his way through his medical contacts in Dublin as he managed to pull together a team who could save the baby. The chances of survival would be even lower for this bambino but there was still hope. Being so ill herself, and with her husband gone, Anne didn't have either the energy or the clout to pull together the right team for the coming birth. Alas, nine days later, the young widow would bear a still born baby, Joseph Patrick Casey, 0, and his little body would be buried beside his father in the loose soil of the family grave.

Jane was only four yet and remembers so much. How could you not? Richard was six and Michael, the eldest, was eight, his father's pride and joy. Now he would have to become the man of the house. Eventually, once the initial shock wore off and Anne came to she told Michael to run down and get the nanny. When no one came, Anne had to traipse down the stairs, her flock trailing behind her, to ask the maids where that aul wan was gone to. They said she was gone to Mass. The aul dragon! She's always gone to mass when she's wanted! Anne struggled back up the stairs and Michael went in with his mammy to see his father, and him there, gone.

#### **Enjoy it while you can**

The early years had been idyllic for the Casey family. The war was over, the world was opening back up, and the prosperous couple had begun to galavant. Dr Michael Augustine Casey had, since his appointment in 1934, been the Medical Officer for the county town of Dungarvan. He was a dispensary doctor and Anne helped make up the medicines, freeing Austie from that drudgery. It was time he did not waste. Incredibly, he was also the **managing director** of the town's two factories, both of which he had set up. In recent years, he found himself and his beautiful wife travelling all around America, buying machines and visiting family in Chicago and Los Angeles. Business was booming now and the men of Dungarvan had steady work, all year round, largely thanks to Austie Casey. The 1950s hadn't happened yet and the mood in Ireland was still hopeful. No sooner were the lovers back from The States and they went on a cruise to Portugal and Madeira. They had a nanny and three maids to help them raise the children, along with Granny May, Anne's mother.

After the tragedy, the four surviving children lived like stray cats, as Laura Ann remembers it, at least until the evening when they'd be home for their daily roast dinner. The older ones had more responsibility and had to face the horror head on. With no father, their mother would be flat out as a dispensary doctor, out in Gaeltacht area of Ring and Old Parish, working like a dog to keep the whole thing going. She only got a paltry stipend in accordance with Austie's second will, which had been changed after one of his heart attacks. **Soon enough, Austie Casey's siblings all began to drop, some of them afflicted by the same heart condition. In ten years' time, only one of the six was still alive. JOE?**

**Dungarvan**

Dungarvan is a self-contained town along the south coast of Ireland, 50k west of Waterford City and 75k east of Cork City. In the 1946 census, it had a population of 5,276 people, and was the seat of the Waterford county council, distinct then from the city council. Its geography looks remarkably similar to that of Dublin, only in miniature. It sits at the centre of a large, protected bay with a river splitting it into two unequal parts. To the north is the village and parish of Abbeyside while Dungarvan is to the south of the River Colligan, a fast-flowing river that rushes down from the mountains inland, also to one side, but to the admittedly north.

Dungarvan does not have a deepwater port however so it always relied on fishing and even that began to dwindle after the establishment of the Free State. In the 1930s, when Fianna Fail decided to dot factories all over the country, Dr Casey managed to convince them the Dungarvan was the perfect location for a tannery. With a river to provide clean water in, and the sea to wash away the noxious waste, its derelict quays were an ideal spot to locate the factory.

## Meeting 

The following day, at noon, a special meeting was convened of the Dungarvan Urban Council, where effusive tributes poured forth from several members of the council. Dr Casey was their leading townsman and captain of local industry, the greatest industrialist Dungarvan has ever known. The man who was responsible for the town's industrial revival, with two flourishing factories. He gave employment, all the year round, to hundreds of men from the town and surrounding countryside, at the best of wages. Without Dr Casey, the town would not be as prosperous, as busy, or even as big as it is. He had been responsible for ending emigration from the town. By the time of the funeral, the following morning, Dr Casey had become perhaps the greatest industrialist in Munster, if not the country.

His good friend Mr M.J Keane noted that very few people realise the strenuous work that Austie had put into the starting of those factories. This contemporary insight is crucial for our understanding of Austie Casey's role in establishing Dickens Leather back in 1935. Without it, one might argue that Austie Casey wasn't the greatest industrialist in even Dungarvan, as there were two bona fide leather men higher up the chain in that factory.

Kennedy O'Brien, a Limerick man, was the first Chairman in the company and he would, over his lifetime, build a small empire across the South-East of Ireland, producing leathers and related products, most notably in nearby Portlaw where he had a large hard leathers factory to complement the soft leathers in Dungarvan.

Reginald Dickens, who gave his name to the Dungarvan tannery, hailed from Northampton, the heart of leather production in England and indeed the world. Dickens' father had set up a tannery around the turn of the century and it was taken over by the elder brothers. Reginald was a younger son who had to go and seek his fortune. When Ireland began to place tariffs on imported goods, hoping to become a self-sufficient state, Reginald was among a band of opportunistic English industrialists who set up shop over here, in adherence with Fianna Fail's jealously regulated isolationist policies. Hoops had to be jumped through and loopholes had to be found, and no one was better at this than the lawyer, Arthur Cox, and the accountant Vincent Crowley, who was on the board of Dickens Leather when it opened. But somebody had to liaise between these Dublin-based middlemen and the ruddy-faced gombeen men of the provinces.

The genius of Austie Casey was in getting a factory to Dungarvan at all. Once it was in the town he could muscle his way to the top and go on to set up a second, offshoot factory. While he couldn't bring the industry insight of either Dickens or O'Brien, Austie Casey had the contacts in the Fianna Fail government of 1932 to convince them to give Dungarvan a factory. He knew Kennedy O'Brien from his factory in Portlaw, and he may well have known Lemass from his time in the IRA.

### **Mountain View House**

Mr and Mrs Michael Augustine Casey lived in a large Georgian house called Mountain View, on a two-acre plot just off O'Connell Street, as you head west out from the square, a few hundred metres. Despite being so close to the town centre, it feels like a country house, and, in its fine original state, it had space aplenty for a family doctor's duties by day and entertaining guests by night.

-   However, it would certainly not have been equipped to deal with the sheer number of people who wanted to pay their respects to deceased before his removal on the Tuesday evening.

-   To the right was a very long dining-room, twenty-six feet by fifteen, and it was separated by an arch from a drawing room with a huge fire place. I suspect that Austie's body would have been laid to rest

Outside, the house was covered all in ivy, head to toe, and around the beautiful non-original porch which has sadly been removed. The staff would have tended to the ample gardens which were walled off from the surroundings, leaving an idyllic space for Austie's young children to wander and play. **Siblings**

Percy would have been the first to get to Mountain View. He was Austie's younger brother and had become is right hand man. He lived on the main street in Dungarvan and still oversaw the family business, a shop that had been owned by their father, Michael J., the much-loved champion of the town's poor, until his death in 1923, and later taken over by his equally-loved wife, Catherine, until her death in 1940. Both of them had huge funerals in the town. Together the Casey brothers set up the Glue and Gelatine factory during The War and, after Austie died, Percy would take on a lot of his responsibilities. He too would **become managing director** of Dickens Leather and would begin to build business connections abroad. Like their father, Percy would become a member of the county council before, like Austie, he would succumb to a heart attack in 1957, **aged just 50.**

The rest of them were as scattered as any large Irish family of the time. Cork, Dublin, England, America. May was married to a Dr Michael O'Shea, and they lived in his native Cork City. Joe, a highly successful accountant, had flown all the way from Los Angeles, where Austie and Anne had visited him on their tour of the States. Rennie had come from Lancashire where he worked as part of a mission among the large Irish community, although he would retire with illness and see out his days in Mountain View, later that decade.

Funeral

Dungarvan shut down on the morning of the funeral and the place was so jammed that the car couldn't move through the crowd. Despite its size, the church couldn't accommodate all the mourners and hundreds had to stand in the precincts. Everyone could attend the burial immediately afterwards as the family plot was right by the entrance to the church. The people in attendance demonstrated the remarkably wide range of activities and contacts Austie had made in a life that paralleled perfectly the Irish nation in the first half of the twentieth century. A very large number in attendance would have been patients of Austie, for whom he had worked so painstakingly and conscientiously since his appointment as the local medical officer in **1932,** after a stint in nearby Cappoquin. There were the factory staff who had carried his body to the church the night before.

After that, the gathering was a diffuse, educated bunch, many of them leaders in the newly formed republic, hailing mostly from the East and South of the country. There were Austie's medical contacts, built up first in University College Dublin, where his studies overlapped with the Revolutionary Period of 1916-23, what he would have called The Troubles. His self-confessed involvement with the IRA in both Dublin and Waterford got him involved in politics and, in particular, Fianna Fail after their establishment and rise to power. It was through these contacts that, in 1935, he could organise the establishment of a large leather factory in Dungarvan, which Minister Sean Lemass would open. Several members attended from Dail Eireann and Seanad Eireann, along with officials from all public bodies in the country. The Waterford County Council members attended en bloc, as arranged at their emergency meeting on the Tuesday.

As a board member of two factories, Austie came into contact with many members of the legal and banking professions, and other managers and directors of various industrial concerns throughout the provinces of Munster and Leinster. It was through the work of such men that Ireland tried to fashion itself as a self-sufficient state, independent of Britain and scarcely connected by trade to Europe.

Austie's involvement in Gaelic games was honoured by the President of the GAA and very large attendance from the Gaels of Waterford, namely the people of the community. **Austie played a huge role in local games.** This era was the high point of Waterford hurling and football. They won the All-Ireland in 1948 and 1949, with Dungarvan being the bulk suppliers, and the Waterfod Foot

In attendance also were also Garda and Army representatives in attendance; the latter may have gotten to know Austie through his eldest brother, Fr. Richard, who had been Head Chaplain in the army until 1948.

Dick would have surely driven down from Skerries where he had, by his energetic standards, retired into a posting as Parish Priest, a role he kept until his death in 1962. It is highly unlikely, given his profession, that he was at home for Easter when Austie died, although he certainly would continue to be a regular guest in Mountain View.

Astonishingly, Dick was the celebrant of the mass (a **Solemn Requiem and High mass**) and was joined by an enormous array of local priests, including those from parishes, to the east and north, of Kilgobnet, Abbeyside, Stradbally, Ballinameela, Kilrossanty, Touraneena, Fourmilewater, Rathgormac(k), Portlaw, and Carrick-on-Suir. From the west and south were priests from Ring and Old Parish, Ardmore, Clashmore, and Cappoquin.
